items.mnemonic_text: A single flat line: the ground, or the number one.
items.description: One stroke, drawn left to right, perfectly flat: a single line of hard-packed dirt stretching all the way across an empty plain, thicker at the ends where the brush pressed down like the ground has been walked on for years. Standing on it, dead centre, is one very smug goat, front hooves together, absolutely nothing else in sight — no hill, no tree, no second goat, no second line. She has decided that this line of earth is the entire world and that she is the only creature in it, and technically, looking at the picture, she is right. When you see this one flat stroke, you are looking at the ground itself, and at the number one standing on it.

items.mnemonic_text: Two flat lines stacked: two.
items.description: Look at the shape: one short flat line lying above one longer flat line, both perfectly level, like two chopsticks set down side by side on a table. That is exactly what happened here — a raccoon in a noodle shop sat down to eat, snapped the top chopstick clean in half against the edge of the bowl, and laid the stubby piece neatly above the whole one anyway, as if nothing had gone wrong. It sits there with a chopstick in neither paw, staring at the pair of sticks on the table, broth cooling. The waiter comes over, counts them, and says the only thing there is to say: that is two.

items.mnemonic_text: Three flat lines stacked: three.
items.description: Look at 三 sideways as a stack of pancakes cooling on a plate, and read it from the top down. The top line is a decent, ordinary pancake; the middle line is shorter because the cook got distracted and poured a stingy little one; the bottom line is the longest because the last of the batter went in all at once and spread out past the edge of the plate. A very serious cat is sitting in front of the stack with a fork in each paw, staring at the pancakes and not blinking, because it has already worked out that it only has two paws and there is one pancake too many. The gap between the lines is the steam still rising between the layers. Whenever you see those three flat lines with the short one in the middle, you are looking at a cat's arithmetic problem, and the answer is three.

items.mnemonic_text: A single vertical stroke: a stick standing up.
items.description: One line, top to bottom, dead straight, with nothing crossing it and nothing hanging off it — the plainest mark you will ever be asked to remember. Picture a pigeon standing in an empty park with that single vertical line held bolt upright in its beak, twice as long as the bird is tall, wobbling like a tightrope walker's pole. It refuses to put the thing down; it hops onto a bench, and the line stays perfectly vertical the whole time, one end scraping the gravel, the other pointing straight at the sky. Every other bird has crumbs and this one has a stick.

items.mnemonic_text: A tiny dot: a single drop.
items.description: Look at the shape: one short stroke, hair-thin where it starts at the top left and swelling as it leans down to the right, exactly the way a bead of liquid hangs and fattens on a rim before it lets go. That is the last of the soy sauce, clinging to the lip of a tipped bottle directly above a freshly ironed white shirt, and the person wearing the shirt is watching it with the flat calm of someone who has already accepted how this morning is going to go. It does not fall in this picture. It just hangs there, pot-bellied and glinting, a single leaning tick of dark liquid suspended over an enormous field of clean white cotton, refusing to commit. Whenever you meet that one fat little slanting stroke, it is that bead a half second before it lands: a drop.

items.mnemonic_text: A flat top with a stem: a lid on top.
items.description: Picture a massive, perfectly flat wooden board slammed over a boiling cauldron to keep the steam in. Right in the exact center, someone has glued a single, ridiculously small peg to grab it with. You have to pinch that tiny vertical peg at the top, heave up the wide horizontal board underneath it, and struggle to remove this highly impractical lid.

items.mnemonic_text: Two legs walking forward: a person.
items.description: The long swooping stroke down to the left is a stretched front leg, and the shorter stroke branching off to the right is a stiff back leg bracing for impact. It looks exactly like someone doing an absurdly wide power stance in the middle of the grocery aisle, refusing to let anyone past. You are looking at the legs of a deeply unbothered person. Be careful not to confuse this with 入, where the right leg is the long, dominant stroke sweeping over the top of the left one. You also need to watch out for 八, where the two strokes are completely detached at the top and do not touch at all.

items.mnemonic_text: A person squeezed against the left side of a kanji.
items.description: Imagine a commuter squeezed so tightly into a train carriage that they have to stand on one perfectly straight leg. That straight vertical drop is their leg planted firmly on the floor to keep balance. Their upper body is shoved over in a sharp diagonal slant to make room for whatever else is cramming into the kanji next to them. This squished shape, permanently shoved to the side of the box, is the symbol for a person (left).

items.mnemonic_text: Two legs left standing without a body.
items.description: Look at these two lines side by side. The left stroke sweeps down smoothly, like a leg stepping confidently forward. The right stroke drops down and violently jerks up into a sharp hook, as if the other foot just caught on a tripwire. What you are looking at is a pair of disembodied, flailing human legs right before a terrible fall.

items.mnemonic_text: A figure ducking through a doorway: to enter.
items.description: A massive steel bunker door swoops down heavily to the right. Someone has propped it open using a single, incredibly flimsy broomstick pushing up from the left. It does not look safe, but crouching down and squeezing under that gap is the only way to enter. Do not confuse this with 人, the character for person. In 人, the long dominant stroke sweeps down to the left, but here the right stroke is the long heavy one resting on top of the short left one.

items.mnemonic_text: Two strokes spreading apart: eight, or splitting.
items.description: Two strokes that never meet: one falls away to the left, one flares away to the right, and between their tops sits a clean open wedge. That wedge is the cut. A watermelon on a picnic table has just been halved in a single stroke, and the two halves are still rocking apart on the boards, leaning outward at exactly the angle of those strokes. Sitting in the pink of the near half, in a tidy row nobody arranged, are eight black seeds. The melon is split, and the count is eight. Do not mix this up with 人, person, whose two strokes join at the top into one peak before the legs spread apart; here the tops never touch, and that open gap between them is the whole point.

items.mnemonic_text: An open-bottomed frame: a wide enclosure.
items.description: The long stroke across the top is a flat lid, and at each end it turns a corner and drops straight down into a short, blunt wall. There is no floor whatsoever. It is a cardboard box turned upside down on the kitchen lino, noticeably wider than it is tall, and it is moving. Two orange duck feet are visible in the gap along the bottom, walking the whole thing at a steady pace toward the fridge. Nobody in the house has mentioned it. What you are looking at is a wide box out for a walk. Watch the two shapes that sit near it: 冖 is a cover, whose legs are stubby little hooks that barely dip below the top line, more a cloth draped over something than walls you could crawl under, and 囗 is an enclosure, sealed shut by a fourth stroke across the bottom, so no duck gets in or out.

items.mnemonic_text: A bent arm flexing: power.
items.description: The stroke comes in across the top like a shoulder, then plunges down and hooks hard back to the left, and that hook is an elbow locked at its tightest possible angle. The short line slicing through it is a tendon standing up under the skin. Picture that one bare arm jammed under the corner of an upright piano wedged in a stairwell, lifting it clear of the step while the mover who was supposed to take the other end waits two stairs up, holding a single cushion. The piano rises. Every string inside hums the same flat note on the way up. That bent, straining arm is power.

items.mnemonic_text: A plus sign: ten, or a cross.
items.description: Someone has driven a single fence post into a muddy field and nailed one long plank straight across it at shoulder height, so the whole thing stands there as one clean cross with nothing else attached. It was meant to become a scarecrow, but the hat and the straw never arrived, so it is just the two boards crossing in the wind. The crows have worked this out. They land on the crossbar one at a time and shuffle sideways to make room, until exactly ten of them are lined up wing to wing and the plank sags in the middle under the weight. The farmer counts them from the kitchen window every morning and gets the same number every morning. One upright, one crossbar, ten crows: the cross that means ten.

items.mnemonic_text: An open square: a mouth or an opening.
items.description: A pug has been mid-bark for four seconds now and has not closed. The left side of its jaw drops straight down, the top lip runs flat across and turns the corner down the other side, and the bottom lip pulls tight underneath, leaving a squat little square parked in the middle of a very confused face. A moth flies in. The pug does not react, because the pug has forgotten how the hinge works, and the moth settles on the tongue like it has found a spare room. That neat square hanging open is a mouth. Do not mix it up with the enclosure 囗, which is drawn large and hollow so other strokes can live inside it, while this square stays small, tucks against the edge of a character, and holds nothing but a moth.

items.mnemonic_text: A closed box: walls around something.
items.description: A bricklayer is finishing a wall around a patch of courtyard: down the left side first, then along the top and around the right corner, then one last course laid straight across the bottom to seal it. Somewhere in the rhythm of the work he forgot to leave a gate. He is now standing in the exact centre of his own completed wall, trowel in one hand and lunch tin in the other, turning slowly to look at four unbroken sides. Nothing gets in, nothing gets out, and the shape has done its one job perfectly: enclosure. The wide box 冂 is these same walls with the bottom missing, open underneath so you could simply walk out, and the mouth 口 is this square shrunk small and kept empty, while 囗 is stretched wide to wrap other strokes inside it.

items.mnemonic_text: A cross pushed into the ground: soil.
items.description: The long vertical is the handle of a spade rammed straight down into a flowerbed, and the short horizontal crossing it near the top is the grip your two hands are closed around. The long horizontal along the bottom is the flat, packed line of soil the blade has completely vanished into. You put your whole weight on the grip and nothing moves, because a mole has taken hold of the blade from underneath and is bracing against you. The two of you hold that pose for a long, silent moment. Then the mole lets go, six fresh holes open in a neat ring around the flowerbed, and you are left standing there holding a handle attached to nothing but earth.

items.mnemonic_text: A figure kneeling gracefully: a woman.
items.description: The two slanting strokes that cross low on the left are a pair of legs folded over each other, one shin tucked across the other, and the line sweeping up from that crossing is a back held straight and a shoulder thrown wide open. The long flat horizontal that cuts through the whole shape is a closed umbrella, hooked through both elbows and held perfectly level, because she fell asleep sitting bolt upright on the station bench and never once loosened her grip. Four pigeons have lined themselves up along the umbrella as though it were installed for exactly that purpose. The last train has come and gone twice. Nobody on the platform is willing to be the one who wakes the woman.

items.mnemonic_text: A swaddled baby with arms out: a child.
items.description: The top stroke is a head far too big for whoever is wearing it, finishing in a hook where one arm has been flung over the playground bar — that dead straight horizontal slicing across the middle of the shape. From the head the vertical drops down and curls into a hook at the very bottom, because the body is wound so tightly in a fleece blanket that there are no feet at the end of it, just a spiral. He has hung there for eleven minutes now, turning slowly, declining every offer of help in a small dignified voice. A patient dog sits directly beneath him, waiting for the blanket to finish unrolling. Nothing about that shape works on an adult, and all of it works on a child.

items.mnemonic_text: Picture a carpenter's flat wooden ruler lying down, with a single tick mark dropping off its right edge — that little notch is where the thumb pins it in place to measure off exactly one inch.
Picture a single tiny seed in the center, with two little hands pinching in from either side to show off just how small it is. Those pinching fingers around the speck are 小 — small.
Look at 山 straight on: three peaks pushing up from one flat ground line, the tall one in the middle flanked by two shorter shoulders. That's the exact jagged silhouette of a mountain against the sky.

Look at 川 and you're standing on a bank watching three long streams of water pour down the page side by side, the outer two bending with the current. Those three vertical channels flowing together are a river.

Picture a steel I-beam standing between two flat concrete slabs: the top and bottom strokes are the slabs, the line down the middle is the beam being lowered into place. That single girder holding the whole thing up is the heart of any construction site.

Picture a snake coiled up tight inside a closed box, its body looping around with just its head poking up through the top — that little gap at the top of 巳 is the head peeking out. When you lift the lid you find it has already curled itself into that shape: a snake, done and waiting.

Picture a hook nailed into the wall, and over that top bar someone has draped a rectangle of fabric so it hangs down in two long folds — the vertical stroke is the drape falling straight to the floor. That limp, hanging shape is a piece of cloth.

Picture a wooden shield with one long vertical plank down the middle and two crossbars nailed across it — that's 干, the flat board a warrior holds up. It's been left out in the sun so long that it's cracked and completely dry.

Picture a single loop of thread pinched at the top and left dangling, its two loose ends trailing off below — so small and fine you have to squint to see it. That flimsy little dangling loop is your tiny thread.
Look at 弓 side-on: those stacked curves are a strip of springy wood bent back on itself, notched top and bottom where the string would hook. Pull it taut and you're holding a bow.

Picture a tall candle standing upright, with a tiny flame flickering off each side of the wick — that thin vertical stroke and its two little side dashes. This candle is the one you light when you're pouring your whole heart into a wish, so 忄is the heart, squeezed slim and standing off to the left.

Picture a wrist at the bottom with the long vertical stroke running up through the palm, while the three horizontal strokes fan out sideways like fingers spread wide — you're looking straight at an open hand.

Picture a vertical arm with three little strokes branching off the side — that's the thumb and fingers curling out. It's a hand reaching in from the left edge of the kanji to grab hold of whatever comes next.
Picture a little window with one bar across the middle — that squat rectangle divided in two is 日, and behind the glass you can see the blazing sun climbing up to start a new day.

Picture a wide-open mouth, that squat outer box, with a single tongue stroke lying flat across the middle — the tongue mid-flap, pushing out a word. That flat tongue in the open mouth is a mouth caught in the act to say something.
See how 月 is a tall window with two bars across the middle? Picture yourself pressing your face to that narrow window at night, and framed perfectly inside it hangs the crescent moon.
See that vertical stroke as a trunk, the horizontal line as a branch spreading out, and the two legs sweeping down as roots gripping the soil — it's a tree standing right there in front of you.

Picture a person slouched sideways in a chair, their body bent into that leaning top stroke while their legs sprawl out below — mouth cracked wide open in a huge, jaw-stretching yawn, so worn out they lack the energy to sit up straight.

Picture a single foot planted flat on the ground, that low horizontal stroke being the sole, with the upright and the little side-stem poking up like the toes and heel dug in. The foot refuses to take one more step — it's frozen mid-stride to stop.

Look at 水 and you'll see a single central stream running straight down, with two smaller trickles splashing off to either side — it's the exact moment a drop hits the surface and sprays outward. That splash frozen mid-air is water.
See those three little strokes stacked down the left side? They're three droplets flicking off a wet paintbrush, one after another, splashing down into a puddle of water.
Picture a single log standing upright, with two sparks flicking off its sides — that's exactly what 火 looks like. Those sparks jumping into the air tell you the whole thing is on fire.
Those four little dots are the glowing embers left at the bottom of a campfire pit, each one a tiny tongue of flame licking up from underneath — the fire burning along the bottom.

See those four strokes crossing at the top like raised arms, with two legs planted wide below? That's your father standing over the barbecue, tongs held high in both hands, proudly announcing dinner is ready.

See that top stroke slanting off to the side? That's the single horn tilting on the head, and the two crossbars below are the sturdy shoulders and back of the animal standing under it — you're looking straight at a cow.

Look at 目 straight on and it's an eye stood on its end: the outer box is the eyelid framing everything, and the two lines inside are the pupil pinched between them, staring right back at you. That vertical eye is exactly what it means — eye.

See that little box tucked under a leaning cliff-face? That's the mouth of a cave in the hillside, and the boxy shape sitting at its base is a big rounded stone that rolled down and came to rest there — one solid stone.

See that flat top line? That's the tabletop of a stone altar, resting on a single strong pillar, with two carved legs splaying out at the base to hold it steady. On its surface you set your offering out for everyone to show — a proper altar.

Look at 田 from above and you're a farmer standing at the edge of your land: two lines cross in the middle like the narrow dirt paths you walk between the plots, chopping the big square into four neat green squares. That grid of squares is your flooded rice field.

See that little roof up top with two dots tucked under it? It's the crooked stone entrance to a hillside, and the wide legs below open outward like a mouth in the rock, swallowing the dark inside — you're staring straight into the cave.

Picture a person planted on a wide flat platform: that top dot is their head, the two little strokes underneath are arms thrown out for balance, and the long bottom line is the solid ground pressing back against their feet — you're watching someone stand.

See those two identical halves standing side by side, each with a short stroke slanting off and a long stroke dropping straight down? Those are two tall stalks with their leaves flicking out — a little grove of bamboo.

Picture a single grain in the middle with husks flying off in every direction — the top strokes spraying up, the bottom strokes kicking down — like a kernel bursting apart the instant it's threshed. That little explosion of scattering pieces is a grain of rice.
Picture a spool up top with a single strand spilling off it, and below, three loose fibers splayed out where the strands have frayed apart — that whole tangle is one piece of thread.

Look at 耳 sideways and you're staring at the side of someone's head: that tall outer frame is the ear's outer rim, and the stack of horizontal lines inside are the ridges and folds curving down into the canal. It's a whole ear stood up on the page.

Picture a butcher's frame, and hanging inside it are two thick slabs strung up side by side on hooks — those are the two little person-shapes tucked under the roof of 肉. It's a window into the shop where the meat hangs.

Picture a mouth flap at the bottom with a little cross sticking up out of it — that's a slab of meat lifting a flag as it pushes its way out past your teeth. That thing wagging out of the mouth is your tongue.

See those two little humps with the line slicing across them? That's two clumps of grass poking up out of the ground, and the horizontal stroke is the soil they're sprouting from — a fresh patch of grass.

Look at 虫: that fat box with the vertical line through it is a plump body skewered on a pin, and the little stroke flicking off the bottom right is a leg twitching — a single insect mounted in a collector's display case.

See that little cross-stroke on top as a coat hanger's hook, and the wide, splayed strokes hanging below it as the sleeves and hem draping down — the whole shape is a shirt hung up to dry, a piece of clothing.
Look at the top box of 見 as a big single eye, and the two strokes underneath are the wobbly legs it walks around on — an eyeball on legs that wanders your room, stopping to see everything it can.

Picture a mouth at the bottom — that little box — stacked with horizontal lines rising off it like speech bubbles floating upward, one on top of another. Every line is another sentence leaving the mouth: this is words spilling out as speech.
See the boxy top as a clam's ridged shell, and the two little legs at the bottom as it tips open — and out spill the coins, because in old Japan these shells were the money.

Picture a person standing under a low horizontal beam, their legs splayed wide into those two trailing strokes at the bottom — they've just sprinted across a scorching desert and their whole sunburned face has flushed a furious, glowing red.

Picture a square kneecap sitting on top, and below it the strokes splay out into a leg that plants down and kicks forward — that little wedge at the bottom is the heel and toes pressing into the ground. The whole shape is one stride caught mid-step: a foot.

Look at 車 straight on: the box in the middle is the body of a cart, the line spearing down through it is the axle running end to end, and the two horizontal bars are the wheels sticking out on either side. It's a wooden cart drawn from above — the original vehicle.

See how the bottom stroke sweeps out flat and long with a little kick at the end? That's a winding road stretching away from you, and the two strokes above it are your own footsteps stepping onto it as you advance forward.

Picture a stack of little rooftops piled up on the right side of the page, each one a bump curving down into the long pole of the road that runs past them — that huddle of houses along the road is a village.
Picture a little roof at the top, and underneath it two tiny nuggets sitting on a stand — this is the covered vault where you pile up your gold.

Picture an old wizard standing tall, his flowing beard streaming down from his chin in a wide fan of strokes that pool at the bottom. That beard has been growing untouched for decades — impossibly, endlessly long.

Look at 門 head-on: two tall pillars framing the left and right, each topped with a little swinging panel, and you can practically hear them creak as they open. Those two heavy doors standing side by side are the entrance to a walled courtyard — a gate.
Picture a window with a flat roof across the top, and behind the glass four little dashes are frozen mid-fall on either side of the frame — that's the rain you're watching streak down the pane.

Picture a garden trellis with a single vine climbing up it, and hanging from that vine is one fat, round moon that's caught the twilight — the whole thing glowing that impossible shade between the sky and the sea, blue-green.

Picture a single drop of milk with a tiny slanted spark of light flicking off its top: that little stroke sitting above the boxy shape is the glint on the drop as it catches the sun. The whole thing is one bright bead of the whitest white you've ever seen.
Look at 馬 side-on: the top box is the head, and those four little legs dashing along the bottom are hooves kicking up dust. Picture that boxy body galloping past you and you're looking at a horse.

Look at 高 from top to bottom: a little roof, then a window box, then another wider room stacked underneath — a slender tower building rising floor by floor into the sky. Every stroke is just one more story added, until the whole thing stands impossibly tall.

Picture an old cast-iron stove: the grid at the top is the fuel packed inside, and the four dots along the bottom are the flames licking up underneath it. Burn it long enough and the whole thing is caked in soot — that's why this shape means black.
